claims.text: Interfaces between dissimilar HEA layers govern resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in multilayer protective coatings.
The interfaces create significant lattice-parameter mismatches.
The interfaces create significant elastic-modulus mismatches.
Lattice-parameter and elastic-modulus mismatches at interfaces act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion reduces creep and suppresses plastic flow over time.
Slight compositional differences between alternating layers produce distinct lattice parameters.
Slight compositional differences between alternating layers produce distinct elastic properties.
Mismatched interfaces create local stress-concentration fields.
Dislocation pile-ups and local stress fields at interfaces impede dislocation motion.
Stress and elevated temperature generate dislocations within the layers during long-term exposure.
Abrupt changes in lattice structure and elastic properties at interfaces force dislocations to halt or change direction.
Interface-induced interruption of dislocation motion delays creep and plastic deformation relative to a homogeneous coating.
Multilayer HEA coatings are expected to exhibit lower creep rates and less accumulated strain than homogeneous coatings of the same overall composition.
After deformation, interface-associated dislocation pile-ups are expected to be more pronounced in multilayer coatings than in homogeneous coatings.
The proposed mechanism applies only while creep is dominant and the layer interfaces remain well-defined.
Interfacial diffusion or breakdown of the layered structure under extreme conditions could invalidate the proposed mechanism.
